title: What Is Natural Language Processing (NLP)? Explained Simply

scenes.narration: When you type good restaurants near me into your phone, how does a machine that only understands numbers know what you mean? The field that makes this possible is called natural language processing, or NLP. By the end of this video, you will know how a computer turns your words into something it can work with.

visual.title: What is NLP?
visual.subtitle: How computers work with human language

scenes.narration: Imagine you receive a letter in a language you do not know. You hire a translator who breaks the letter into small pieces, looks each piece up in a dictionary, and then works out what the whole letter is saying. NLP works in a similar way. A computer cannot read words the way we do, so natural language processing turns language into pieces and numbers it can work with, step by step.
cues: breaks the letter into small pieces
looks each piece up in a dictionary
works out what the whole letter

scenes.narration: Step one is tokenization. The computer splits your sentence into small pieces called tokens. A token is often a whole word, but it can also be part of a word or a punctuation mark. Then each token is swapped for a number, because computers work with numbers, not letters. The numbers on screen are only examples. Every system has its own numbering.

A number alone does not tell the computer what a word means. So the next step gives each token a long list of numbers, called an embedding. You can think of an embedding as a position on a map of meaning. Words used in similar ways end up close together: cat near dog, car near truck, pizza near rice. A real map has hundreds or thousands of dimensions, but the idea is the same. Closeness means similar use.

cues.map: position on a map of meaning

scenes.narration: Step three is learning. A model is trained on huge amounts of text. It learns patterns, such as which words tend to appear together, and how word order changes meaning.

visual.title: Step 3: Learning patterns
items: Trained on huge amounts of text
Learns how word order changes meaning

cues: which words tend to appear together

scenes.narration: Once trained, the model handles new text in the same steps. When you give it new text, your words become tokens. The tokens become numbers. The model works with those numbers. And then it produces an answer, such as a translation, a label, or a reply.

You use NLP every day. Search engines use it to understand what you are looking for. Your email uses it to filter spam. Phones use it to autocomplete messages and to turn speech into text. Translation tools and chatbots are built on it too.

Language is hard for computers. The word bank can mean the side of a river or a place for money, and only the context tells you which. The sentence, I saw her duck, could be about a bird or about someone bending down. Sarcasm and slang trip up even the best systems. And languages with less text available online, often including many African languages, usually get weaker tools than English.

So does a computer truly understand language the way you do? Researchers still debate that. What we know is that these systems are very good at finding patterns in text, and that is often enough to be useful.

Let's recap. One: NLP helps computers work with human language by turning it into numbers. Two: the steps are tokens, then embeddings, then a trained model that finds patterns. Three: you already use it in search, translation, spam filters, and chatbots.
